Fit a two-level latent profile model

Source: R/multilpa.R
multilpa.Rd

Multilevel latent profile analysis describes heterogeneity among observations and among the groups in which they are nested. Examples include repeated measurements within individuals and students within schools. Observation-level profiles describe patterns in the indicators, while group-level classes describe differences in the probabilities of those profiles.

In the standard model, profile definitions are shared across group classes: a given profile has the same indicator means and covariance structure in every group class. Group classes therefore differ in their profile composition. Observations within the same group can belong to different profiles, with their membership probabilities depending on the group's latent class.

multilpa() estimates the measurement parameters, conditional profile probabilities, group-class proportions, and posterior membership probabilities at both levels. The default specification uses Gaussian indicators with diagonal within-profile covariance matrices. Alternative specifications support other covariance structures, discrete or mixed indicators, and predictors of latent membership.

Usage

multilpa(
  data,
  vars,
  id,
  n_profiles,
  n_group_classes = 2L,
  profile_covariates = character(),
  group_covariates = character(),
  variance_model = c("varying", "equal"),
  n_starts = 10L,
  max_iter = 1000L,
  tol = 1e-08,
  min_variance = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  start = NULL,
  missing = c("error", "fiml"),
  profile_slopes = c("shared", "group_class"),
  covariance_model = c("diagonal", "full"),
  categorical = character(),
  min_probability = 1e-10,
  time = NULL,
  fixed = character(),
  centering = c("none", "person", "grand"),
  volume = NULL,
  shape = NULL,
  orientation = NULL,
  model = NULL,
  select_start = c("likelihood", "converged"),
  prior = NULL,
  noise = FALSE,
  acceleration = c("squarem", "none"),
  family = c("profiles", "additive", "dispersion", "additive_dispersion",
    "restricted_cross_level", "full_cross_level"),
  between_variance = c("varying", "equal"),
  weights = NULL,
  ordinal = character(),
  count = character(),
  count_model = c("poisson", "negative_binomial"),
  count_dispersion = c("varying", "equal"),
  scaling = c("none", "person", "grand"),
  drop_empty = TRUE,
  cores = 1L,
  local_dependence = character(),
  direct_effects = character(),
  search = NULL,
  n_screen = NULL,
  boundary = c("allow", "exclude")
)

Arguments

data

A data frame containing the indicators and the group identifier.

vars

Unique character vector of indicator column names. Columns not named in categorical, ordinal or count are continuous indicators.

id

Name of the group identifier column. Character, factor and numeric identifiers are supported; missing identifiers are not. id has no default: omitting it raises latents_bad_argument.

id = NULL fits a single-level model: each row is its own unit, the observations are independent, and n_group_classes is one. The fit raises a latents_single_level message. Methods for extracting results, visualization and inference remain available. The internal unit column is named .observation; it is not returned by get_results(x, "data"), and a data that already has a column of that name raises latents_bad_data. Requesting more than one group class with id = NULL raises latents_bad_argument.

n_profiles

Positive integer number of individual profiles.

n_group_classes

Positive integer number of latent group classes (default 2). With id = NULL it is one, and any other value is an error.

profile_covariates, group_covariates

Names of numeric columns of data that predict individual-profile and group-class membership through multinomial logits, with the last class as reference. Naming either fits the one-step maximum-likelihood covariate model and returns a multilpa_covariates object. Profile intercepts differ by group class; profile slopes are shared across group classes unless profile_slopes = "group_class". A group covariate must be constant within each group. Covariates enter in their supplied units, without centring or scaling. The covariate model rejects start and fixed; it accepts missing = "fiml" for the indicators, but the covariates must be complete. three_step() and r3step() are the staged alternatives.

variance_model

"varying" (the default; profile-specific variances or covariance matrices) or "equal" (shared across profiles).

n_starts

Positive integer number of EM starts (default 10). The first start is deterministic: Ward's hierarchical clustering of the standardized indicators (on at most 2000 evenly spaced rows), each cluster initialized with its own means and variances, and, with more than one group class, Ward's clustering of the groups' profile compositions. The remaining starts are k-means from random centres. A supplied start replaces the first start, and the remaining starts are random. With start and max_iter = 0, exactly one start is evaluated regardless of n_starts. Zero-weight units do not contribute to initialization. For search = "emEM", n_starts is the number of final optimization runs, including the protected first start (see search).

max_iter

Nonnegative integer maximum number of EM updates per start (default 1000). max_iter = 0 performs no update: with start, the model is evaluated at exactly those values, for example to score them with logLik(); without start, the random initializations are evaluated and the one with the highest log likelihood is returned.

tol

Positive convergence tolerance (default 1e-8). EM has converged when one step (or SQUAREM cycle) changes the log likelihood by no more than tol times the number of observed indicator values (each non-missing cell in a row of positive weight, with a minimum count of one). The tolerance is therefore expressed per observed indicator value.

min_variance

Lower bound on each variance, or on each covariance eigenvalue under full covariance; the fit is then constrained maximum likelihood. NULL (the default) sets it to 1e-6 times the smallest sample variance of the continuous indicators (observed values in rows of positive weight, on the scale fitted, after any centring and scaling), so that the default bound adapts to the measurement scale. A numeric value specifies an absolute bound in squared indicator units. The bound used is stored as min_variance on the fit. Estimates at the bound are reported and raise a warning.

seed

Optional random seed: any integer set.seed() accepts, including negative integers. When supplied, the caller's random-number state is restored on exit.

start

Optional list of means and variances (profiles by indicators), profile_probabilities (group classes by profiles), and group_probabilities (vector). Starting probabilities must be positive. For full covariance, supply covariances (indicators by indicators by profiles); variances may then be omitted, or must match their diagonals. A categorical model also takes response_probabilities, a list of one profiles-by-categories matrix per indicator named in categorical. The list is matched by position unless it is labelled: when its elements are named after the indicators, or its columns after the categories, each block is matched to the indicator and category its labels name. A label naming an indicator or category the fit does not have raises latents_bad_start.

missing

"error" (the default) rejects missing indicators; "fiml" maximizes the observed-data likelihood under an ignorable missingness mechanism (MAR), integrating missing indicators out rather than filling them in. This also holds with membership covariates; the covariates themselves must be complete (latents_bad_data).

profile_slopes

"shared" (the default) gives each profile covariate one slope per profile logit, common to every group class. "group_class" estimates separate slopes in each group class (a cross-level interaction), reported with terms such as z:group_class_1; it multiplies the number of slope parameters by n_group_classes, each set estimated from the groups in its class. Naming it without profile_covariates raises latents_bad_argument.

covariance_model

"diagonal" (the default) assumes conditional independence; "full" estimates within-profile residual covariances.

categorical

Character vector naming indicators to treat as categorical. Each is modelled by unrestricted, profile-specific response probabilities over its observed categories (the latent class measurement model); binary, ordinal and unordered indicators are handled by the same parameterization. Numeric, integer, logical, character and factor columns are accepted. Indicators not named here stay Gaussian, so naming a subset fits a mixed-mode model.

min_probability

Positive lower bound on every categorical response probability (default 1e-10), constraining the maximum-likelihood problem as min_variance does for Gaussian indicators.

time

Optional name of a column giving each observation's position within its group, such as a wave, occasion or course number. It is not used in estimation; it is stored for get_results(x, "sequences"), get_results(x, "sequence_summary") and plot(what = "sequences"). Values must be complete and unique within each group, and are ordered as sort() orders them: numbers numerically, a factor by its levels, and character strings alphabetically. Numbers stored as text whose alphabetical order is not their numeric order ("2", "10"), and numbered labels sharing their text around the number whose alphabetical order is not the numbers' ("T2", "T10"; "week 2", "week 10"), raise latents_bad_time (also latents_bad_data); give the order with factor(levels = ) or zero-pad the numbers. Zero-padded numbers and ISO dates are accepted.

fixed

Character vector naming measurement blocks to hold at the values in start instead of estimating them: any of "means", "variances" and "response_probabilities", or "measurement" for every block the model has. Under covariance_model = "full", "variances" holds the residual covariance matrices. A fixed block retains its supplied values in every start and is not counted in n_parameters, so the result is a different model, not a different starting point. start must contain the named blocks; starting_values(fit, what = "measurement") produces them, and fit_staged() performs the two-stage workflow in one call. The mixing parameters cannot be held.

centering

How to centre the continuous indicators before fitting. "none" (the default) fits them as supplied. "person" subtracts each group's own mean from its rows, so values are deviations from the unit's average, the profiles describe within-unit change rather than level, and the group classes are types of change pattern rather than types of unit (the person-mean-centred within-person design; Quintana, 2021; Voelkle, Brose, Schmiedek, & Lindenberger, 2014). "grand" subtracts one mean per indicator, which moves the origin without changing the within-group structure. The offsets are stored on the fit, so get_results(x, "data") returns the supplied columns and row-alignment checks still apply. "person" raises latents_bad_data when it leaves an indicator constant, as happens when a unit has one observation of it.

volume, shape, orientation

The covariance structure in its three components. Each profile's covariance decomposes as Sigma_k = lambda_k * D_k * A_k * D_k', with volume lambda_k = |Sigma_k|^(1/d), orientation D_k (eigenvectors) and shape A_k (diagonal, determinant one). Constraining the three across profiles gives the fourteen models mclust names with three letters, all of which are available.

volume is "equal" or "varying". shape is "equal", "varying" or "spherical"; "spherical" makes the variance equal across indicators within a profile and leaves no orientation to constrain. orientation is "axis" (a diagonal covariance), "equal" (one orientation shared by every profile) or "varying". Each defaults to NULL, which follows variance_model and covariance_model.

volumeshapeorientationmodel
equalspherical—EII
varyingspherical—VII
equal/varyingequal/varyingaxisEEI, VEI, EVI, VVI
equal/varyingequal/varyingequalEEE, VEE, EVE, VVE
equal/varyingequal/varyingvaryingEEV, VEV, EVV, VVV

The estimates are those of Celeux and Govaert (1995); EVE and VVE, which combine a shared orientation with a free shape, have no closed form and use the minorize-maximize step of Browne and McNicholas (2014). Parameter counts match mclust's for all fourteen.

Structures other than EEI, VVI, EEE and VVV are maximized across all profiles jointly and cannot be combined with a held variances block. parameter_inference() reports Wald standard errors for all fourteen, computed in the structure's free coordinates (log volumes, determinant-one log shapes and orientations) and transformed to the reported variances and covariances by the delta method; method = "bootstrap" is also available for all fourteen.

model

The covariance structure as an mclust code, one of "EII", "VII", "EEI", "VEI", "EVI", "VVI", "EEE", "VEE", "EVE", "VVE", "EEV", "VEV", "EVV", "VVV". The letters give the volume, shape and orientation, each equal (E) or varying (V) across profiles, with I for axis-aligned (no covariances). These are the codes enumerate_classes() takes. Use it instead of variance_model/covariance_model or volume/shape/orientation, not together with them.

select_start

Rule for selecting a fitted solution. "likelihood" (the default) selects among starts within tol * max(1, n_observed) of the highest log likelihood, preferring converged starts within this set. Here n_observed counts observed indicator values in positive-weight rows. "converged" restricts selection to converged starts when any are available; otherwise it uses all starts. Remaining ties are resolved by start order. Convergence is required for Wald inference but does not establish identification or global optimality. summary() and get_results(fit, "starts") report the individual starts. The reported replication count includes final-stage starts within 1e-6 * max(1, n_observed) of the selected log likelihood, where n_observed counts observed indicator values in rows of positive sampling weight, as in the EM stopping rule. This absolute likelihood-gap tolerance is independent of measurement units and of tol, since a start stopped by the EM rule can still lie several steps below its maximum. It is stored as replication_tolerance and does not select a start.

prior

NULL (the default) for maximum likelihood, or a prior_control() object for maximum a posteriori estimation of the Gaussian means and covariances under the conjugate prior of Fraley and Raftery (2007). Hyperparameters use the data-dependent defaults of mclust::defaultPrior(), and updates follow the conventions described in prior_control(). Available for EII, VII, EEI, VEI, EVI, VVI, EEE, EEV, VEV and VVV (mclust has no prior for VEE, EVE, VVE and EVV), with complete continuous indicators and without fixed or membership covariates; otherwise latents_unsupported_prior is raised. The mixing proportions have no prior. As in mclust, the fit's log_likelihood is the unpenalized log likelihood at the posterior mode, and aic, bic and their variants are computed from it with the usual parameter count. Convergence uses the change described under tol; because a MAP step can lower that likelihood, the decrease check made under maximum likelihood is not applied. parameter_inference(method = "wald") raises latents_unsupported_inference for such a fit, because the score is not zero at a posterior mode; method = "bootstrap" refits every resample with the same prior. The fit stores the request as prior and the resolved hyperparameters, in the indicators' units (centred, under centering), as prior_parameters.

noise

FALSE (the default), or TRUE to add a noise component: a mixture component with constant density 1 / V over the hypervolume V of the data, which absorbs outliers and scatter that no Gaussian profile explains (Banfield & Raftery, 1993; mclust's initialization = list(noise = ) and Vinv). V is mclust's hypvol(): the smaller of the volumes of the data's axis-aligned and principal-component-aligned bounding boxes. The component has no measurement parameters; its mixing proportion is estimated with the others, and, as in mclust, it adds two parameters (the proportion and the hypervolume), following mclust's parameter-count convention. A random start assigns probability 0.1 to noise. A supplied start includes noise_probability alongside profile_probabilities, the two summing to one. Available for complete continuous indicators with one group class (id = NULL or n_group_classes = 1), under any of the fourteen covariance structures, with or without prior; otherwise latents_unsupported_noise is raised. In the fit the noise component is profile 0, as in mclust's classification: subject_profiles is 0 for an observation assigned to it, get_results(fit, "assignments") adds a posterior_noise column, get_results(fit, "posteriors") and get_results(fit, "profile_probabilities") have profile-0 rows, and the classification diagnostics count it as a class. means, variances, covariances, profile_probabilities and subject_posteriors describe the Gaussian profiles only, so the last two sum to one minus the noise share; the fit adds noise_probability, noise_posteriors, n_noise and hypervolume. parameter_inference(), three_step(), r3step(), bootstrap_lrt(), starting_values(), bivariate residuals, fit_staged() and the posterior plots raise latents_unsupported_noise for such a fit.

acceleration

"squarem" (the default) accelerates EM with SQUAREM (Varadhan & Roland, 2008): each cycle extrapolates along the last two EM steps in unit-free coordinates (means divided by reference standard deviations, variances and covariances by the corresponding products; probabilities unchanged). Reference standard deviations use observed values in rows of positive sampling weight. Each cycle ends with an ordinary EM step and reverts to the EM update when the extrapolated point would lower the likelihood, so the iteration stays monotone. Convergence is assessed over a complete cycle. "none" runs ordinary EM. iterations and max_iter count EM steps under either setting. Fits with prior, and models with membership covariates, always use plain EM. For EVE and VVE, whose shared orientation has no closed form, each EM iteration takes a fixed number of warm-started orientation steps (a generalized EM step) under either setting, which keeps every iteration monotone and the EM map a fixed function, as SQUAREM requires.

family

The model family. "profiles" (the default) is the model described above: individual profiles whose prevalences differ across group classes. Three group-class-only families have no individual profiles (Houle, Morin & Harvey, 2026): each group has a Gaussian intercept per indicator, drawn from its group class's distribution, and its members vary around it.

  • "additive": group classes differ in their means (and, optionally, in between-group variances); one within-group variance per indicator is shared by every class.

  • "dispersion": group classes differ in their within-group variances; means and between-group variances are shared.

  • "additive_dispersion": group classes differ in means and in within-group variances.

These families take only data, vars, id, n_group_classes, between_variance, n_starts, max_iter, tol, min_variance, seed, weights, search and n_screen; any other argument raises latents_bad_argument. Groups of sampling weight zero are not part of the sample: the identification checks, starting values, counts, entropy and classification tables use only the groups of positive weight, though every group still receives a posterior. Indicators must be complete and continuous, and at least one group must have more than one row (latents_unidentified otherwise). Between variances estimated at zero are reached by a boundary maximization with a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker check and flagged (latents_boundary); interior fits are finished by Newton steps. The result has class multilpa_additive; bic uses the number of groups and bic_individual the number of rows. It is read with get_results(); summary(), plot(), coef(), vcov(), confint() and parameter_inference() work on it, enumerate_classes() compares families through its family argument, and bootstrap_lrt() tests one number of group classes against another. These families are experimental: parameter_inference(method = "bootstrap") raises latents_unsupported_inference, and missing indicators (latents_bad_data), missing, membership covariates and ordinal or count indicators (latents_bad_argument) are not available. See the group-class and cross-level models article.

Two cross-level families estimate individual profiles and group classes from the same indicators, following the manifest-aggregation specification of Houle et al. (2026, supplement): each group's means of the indicators are between-level indicators of its group class, with class-specific means and variances.

  • "restricted_cross_level": profile prevalences are the same in every group class, so profiles and group classes are estimated separately; the profile composition of each class is reported descriptively.

  • "full_cross_level": profile prevalences differ across group classes (as in "profiles"), and the group means also inform the classes.

These take data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, variance_model (individual profiles), between_variance (group classes), n_starts, max_iter, tol, min_variance, seed and weights. The group means are computed from the same ratings, so the likelihood is the specification's working likelihood: comparable between cross-level fits of the same data, not with the other families. Standard errors are not available (latents_unsupported_inference). The result has class multilpa_cross_level, read with get_results(). Its get_results(fit, "profiles") table ends with a prevalence column: each individual profile's prevalence (estimated and shared for the restricted family, the class-weighted marginal for the full family) and, on the group-class rows, the class weight.

between_variance

For the additive and additive-dispersion families: "varying" (the default) estimates between-group variances per group class, "equal" one set shared by all classes. The dispersion family holds them equal and rejects "varying". For the cross-level families, the variances of the group means within each group class.

weights

NULL, or the name of a numeric column of data holding a sampling weight for each independent unit: each id group of a two-level fit, each row of a single-level one. A two-level weight must be constant within its group (latents_bad_weights otherwise); within-unit weights are not supported. The fit maximizes the pseudo log likelihood sum_j w_j log L_j (Skinner, 1989) with the weights scaled to sum to the number of units of positive weight, as Mplus scales to the sample size, so integer weights give the fit to the data with each unit repeated that many times and the criteria stay on the sample's scale. A unit of weight zero is not part of the sample: it changes no estimate, likelihood, sample size, entropy or criterion, sets neither the grand offset nor the grand scale of centering/scaling = "grand", and is not classified. Nor does it define a category: a categorical, ordinal or paired (local_dependence) value seen only on units of weight zero is not a category of the fit and has no parameter, and an indicator constant among the positive-weight units is rejected regardless of zero-weight values. Under missing = "error", a missing categorical, ordinal or count value on a unit of weight zero is not rejected; a missing continuous value is. Standard errors are sandwich estimates: parameter_inference() defaults to vcov_type = "robust" and rejects "observed" and "opg" (latents_unsupported_weights), and method = "bootstrap" resamples the units with their weights. Classification tables report each unit's own posterior; effective counts and proportions are weighted. bootstrap_lrt(), three_step(), r3step(), prior and noise reject a weighted fit. Weights are supported with every family, membership covariates, categorical indicators and missing = "fiml".

ordinal

Names of indicators in vars to model as ordinal: an (ordered) factor, or integers, whose categories are ordered by factor level or by value. Each follows an adjacent-category logit with category intercepts shared by every profile and one location per profile, log P(k | c) / P(k - 1 | c) = a_k - a_(k-1) + eta_c, with the last profile's location fixed at zero: (K - 1) + (C - 1) parameters per indicator, against C (K - 1) for a categorical one. This is Latent GOLD's default ordinal model, against which it is checked. The category probabilities and locations are returned by get_results(fit, "ordinal"). A factor level never observed in the data raises the latents_unused_category warning; droplevels() removes it.

count

Names of indicators in vars holding non-negative whole numbers, modelled as Poisson with one mean per profile (or negative binomial, see count_model); the means are returned by get_results(fit, "count_means"). Ordinal and count indicators support missing = "fiml", weights, two-level fits, membership covariates, Wald and bootstrap inference, bootstrap_lrt(), predict() and lta(). start, fixed, prior and noise do not accept them (latents_unsupported_indicator), and the group-class and cross-level families do not support them (latents_bad_argument).

count_model

"poisson" (the default) or "negative_binomial": NB2, with mean mu and variance mu + alpha mu^2, for counts with greater variance than a Poisson within a profile (Latent GOLD's poisson overdispersed). A dispersion estimated at zero is the Poisson limit, a boundary fit (latents_boundary warning; Wald inference is rejected there).

count_dispersion

For count_model = "negative_binomial": one dispersion per profile ("varying", the default) or one shared by every profile ("equal").

scaling

How to scale the continuous indicators before fitting, at the same levels as centering. "none" (the default) fits them as supplied. "grand" divides each indicator by its standard deviation over all observations; "person" divides each group's values by that group's own standard deviation. With the matching centring these are z-scores: centering = "grand", scaling = "grand" standardizes each indicator over the sample, and centering = "person", scaling = "person" standardizes it within each unit. Standard deviations use the observed values with denominator n - 1. The scales are stored on the fit with the centring offsets, so get_results(x, "data") returns the supplied columns, and predict() scales new units by their own standard deviation under "person" and by the fitted standard deviation under "grand". Means, variances and covariances are reported in standard-deviation units. The log likelihood and every information criterion are those of the scaled values, so only fits with the same centring and scaling are comparable. A standard deviation that is zero or undefined (under "person", a unit observed once on an indicator or always giving the same value) raises latents_bad_data. Under EEI, VEI, EVI, VVI, EEE, VEE, EVV and VVV, whose family is unchanged when each indicator is rescaled, grand scaling changes only the units of the estimates and adds the density Jacobian to each start's log likelihood. SQUAREM uses unit-free coordinates, so its search path is equivariant in exact arithmetic when variance bounds are inactive or transformed with the model. Rounding near convergence can still change iteration counts, and nearly tied starts can change the selected labelling. A scalar variance or eigenvalue floor is not generally preserved by unequal indicator rescaling. Under the spherical EII and VII, which impose one variance on every indicator, and under EEV, VEV, EVE and VVE, which share eigenvalues or eigenvectors across profiles (neither survives rescaling the indicators by different factors), it changes the solution. Under centering = "person" with scaling = "person", a group with only two observations of an indicator becomes exactly -1/sqrt(2) and 1/sqrt(2) on it: such groups raise latents_atomic_groups, and when every group is like that the fit is rejected with latents_bad_data.

drop_empty

TRUE (the default) or FALSE: how the reported statistics treat rows whose every indicator is missing, and groups consisting only of such rows. This setting affects reporting, not estimation. With TRUE they are excluded, as in Mplus, from the individual and group sample sizes of the information criteria, from relative entropy, AvePP and the entropy term of ICL, AWE and CLC, from the classification tables and diagnostic plots, and from the effective class counts. Row-aligned assignment and posterior tables retain these units but report their classifications and posterior probabilities as NA. A partially observed row remains classified, and an empty row in an informative group can retain its group-class assignment. With FALSE every row and group is counted in those statistics, except in the individual sample size of a multilpa() fit, which excludes such rows either way. Units of sampling weight zero are excluded from every count and entropy term under either setting. compare_models() and bootstrap_lrt() do not compare fits made with different drop_empty. The setting is stored on the fit and passed on by enumerations and refits; it has no effect on data without such rows.

cores

Number of processor cores for the random starts (default 1). The starting values are drawn in order in the current process and only the EM iterations are distributed, so the result is identical to cores = 1. Under search = "emEM" both the screening of the pool and the final runs are distributed; the screening is most of the time of an emEM fit, so a large model or data set gains most. Workers are forked processes on macOS and Linux, and a socket cluster on Windows and on macOS with Apple's Accelerate BLAS, as in enumerate_classes(). Lost worker results are retried once with half as many workers (rounded up). One latents_worker_lost warning reports losses and recovery; starts still lost are recorded as failed. Socket workers retain completed chunks, but tasks within a failed chunk may also be retried. Models with membership covariates run their starts on one core. To fit many models, give cores to enumerate_classes(), which shares its worker pool across candidates and their starts for models without membership covariates or joined categorical local_dependence pairs. Other fitting engines use one task per candidate.

local_dependence

Pairs of indicators that stay associated within each class, written "item1:item2" (several as a character vector). A continuous indicator pair has a covariance estimated within each class (one shared covariance with variance_model = "equal"), every other covariance staying zero: the covariance Latent GOLD fits with item1 <-> item2 | Cluster. It is not combined with covariance_model, model or the structure arguments, covariates, time, prior, noise or held variances. A pair of categorical indicators is modelled jointly within each class. Each such pair becomes one categorical indicator, named "item1:item2", whose categories are every combination of the two items' categories (the full grid: an unobserved combination is estimated on the min_probability floor and counted as a parameter, so each class has K1 K2 - 1 of them), so every class has its own joint distribution of the pair: the class-specific association Latent GOLD fits with item1 <-> item2 | Cluster. The other indicators stay independent given the class. get_results(fit, "local_dependence") reports each class's joint probabilities beside their values under independence; predict(), parameter_inference(data = ) and the other functions that take data join the pair in the caller's data. Under missing = "fiml" a row observing one item of a pair and not the other contributes the observed item, the pair's joint distribution summed over the missing one, which is the observed-data likelihood under MAR. A pair that mixes a categorical and a continuous indicator, that names an indicator twice or that shares an indicator with another pair raises latents_bad_argument; a categorical item of a pair whose categories contain ":" raises latents_bad_data. Default: none.

direct_effects

Direct effects of covariates on continuous indicators, written "indicator ~ covariate" (several covariates joined with +, several indicators as a character vector). The covariate moves the indicator's mean by the same amount in every profile, y = mean_k + b z + e (Bandeen-Roche et al., 1997), so a difference in the indicator that the covariate explains is not read as a difference between profiles: the direct effect Latent GOLD fits with y <- 1 + Cluster + z. Covariates are numeric columns of data, observed in every row (code a categorical covariate as indicator columns), and enter with their values as given, so means are the profile means at a covariate value of zero; centre a covariate first to read them at its mean. The effects are estimated with the profiles (a conditional maximization step in EM; Meng & Rubin, 1993), have standard errors in parameter_inference() (parameter direct_effect, term "indicator:covariate"), and are reported by get_results(fit, "direct_effects"). predict() and the functions that take data read the covariates from it. Direct effects need a diagonal covariance (EEI or VVI) and are not combined with local_dependence between continuous indicators, profile_covariates, group_covariates, time, prior, noise, fixed, start, centering or scaling; those, a term that is not "indicator ~ covariate", and an indicator that is not continuous raise latents_bad_argument, and a covariate that is absent, not numeric, missing or constant raises latents_bad_data. Default: none.

search

How the starts are found: NULL (the default), "kmeans" or "emEM". NULL uses "emEM" when every profile shares one covariance matrix (EII, EEI, EEE with continuous indicators), which removes the isolated-profile covariance-collapse mechanism. Shared covariances can still hit their floor on degenerate or over-extracted data; inspect the boundary diagnostics. The default is "kmeans" otherwise, including categorical-only models and the group-class families. The selected search strategy is recorded on the fit. "kmeans" runs n_starts starts to convergence: Ward's clustering first, then k-means from random centres. "emEM" screens a pool of n_screen starts by a short EM run each and runs n_starts selected starts to convergence (Biernacki, Celeux & Govaert, 2003). The first start (Ward's clustering, or supplied starting values) is retained for final optimization if its screening succeeds; remaining starts are selected by screening likelihood. Thus n_starts = 1 finalizes Ward's start whenever it screens successfully, even if another screened start has a higher likelihood. With a supplied start and n_starts = 1, screening is skipped entirely. The pool begins with the kmeans search's own starts, drawn in the same order, followed by random partitions of the rows and random rows as class centres, and get_results(fit, "starts") gives every start of the pool with its kind, its stage and its likelihood after screening. Either search reports the start with the highest likelihood among those run to convergence (subject to select_start and boundary). With profile-specific variances that maximum can correspond to a nearly degenerate component concentrated on a few observations (McLachlan & Peel, 2000, section 3.10). More extensive searches can identify such solutions more often. A variance at min_variance produces a latents_boundary warning; use boundary = "exclude" to exclude these starts when an interior solution is available. Low effective Gaussian profile membership produces the heuristic warning latents_thin_profiles. get_results(fit, "gaussian_diagnostics") reports continuous covariance and support measures without an automatic spike cutoff or changing the selected start. Neither a warning's absence nor a repeated likelihood establishes a regular or globally optimal solution.

n_screen

For search = "emEM", the number of starts screened, at least n_starts. NULL (the default) screens five times n_starts. The protected first start is included in the n_starts final optimization runs. Increasing n_screen does not increase that number. A single supplied start with n_starts = 1 disables screening. A value with search = "kmeans", or one below n_starts, raises latents_bad_argument.

boundary

Whether a start with a variance at min_variance (a covariance eigenvalue, under full covariance) may be reported. "allow" (the default) permits it, as Mplus does, with a latents_boundary warning. "exclude" sets such starts aside and applies select_start to the rest; for models without covariates, the boundary column of the starts table identifies them. When every start is at the bound, the best is reported with a latents_all_starts_boundary warning. A Gaussian profile can increase the likelihood without limit by shrinking around one observation, so the size of that gain is set by min_variance rather than by the data, and more starts make such a solution more likely to be found. Categorical indicators have no variances and are unaffected.

Value

A multilpa object containing means, variances, optional covariances (indicators by indicators by profiles), profile_probabilities, group_probabilities, posterior matrices, classifications, log likelihood, information criteria, restart diagnostics and convergence history. Individual rows retain their input order; groups keep first-occurrence order. bic and bic_groups use the observed group count; bic_individual uses n_informative, the number of rows with at least one observed indicator. These are alternative conventions, not interchangeable criteria. boundary identifies variance bounds; small_classes flags a profile or group class whose effective membership (effective_profile_counts, effective_group_counts, weighted for a fit with weights) is below one, in which case the fit warns with latents_small_classes. The fit carries no standard errors: parameter_inference() computes them, and bootstrap_lrt() tests nested models. Global optimality is not guaranteed for any n_starts. as.data.frame() returns the tidy tables, selected by what.

Details

Infinite and constant observed indicators are rejected; each indicator must have at least two distinct observed values. No rows are silently dropped. Under FIML, fully missing individuals contribute no direct measurement likelihood but receive posterior probabilities from their group's information. The individual-level BIC excludes these rows through n_informative; the treatment of fully missing groups follows drop_empty. Missing patterns can prevent parameter identification; no general identification guarantee is made. Only initialization fills missing values with indicator means; EM uses conditional Gaussian sufficient statistics and observed marginal densities. More than one group class requires more than one profile and at least one group with more than one individual; these checks are necessary but do not establish identification. A model of complete categorical and ordinal indicators alone, with one group class, warns (latents_unidentified) when it has more free parameters than its contingency table has free cells (negative degrees of freedom), which no data can identify (Goodman, 1974). Start selection follows select_start; the default can return a solution that has not converged. Inspect the converged flag and the starts table before interpreting the model. Profile and group-class labels are arbitrary.

References

Vermunt, J. K. (2003). Multilevel latent class models. Sociological Methodology, 33, 213–239. doi:10.1111/j.0081-1750.2003.t01-1-00131.x.

Goodman, L. A. (1974). Exploratory latent structure analysis using both identifiable and unidentifiable models. Biometrika, 61(2), 215–231. doi:10.1093/biomet/61.2.215.

Banfield, J. D., & Raftery, A. E. (1993). Model-based Gaussian and non-Gaussian clustering. Biometrics, 49, 803–821. doi:10.2307/2532201.

Bandeen-Roche, K., Miglioretti, D. L., Zeger, S. L., & Rathouz, P. J. (1997). Latent variable regression for multiple discrete outcomes. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 92(440), 1375–1386.

Meng, X.-L., & Rubin, D. B. (1993). Maximum likelihood estimation via the ECM algorithm: A general framework. Biometrika, 80(2), 267–278. doi:10.1093/biomet/80.2.267.

Houle, S. A., Morin, A. J. S., & Harvey, J.-F. (2026). Multilevel latent profile analyses: A comprehensive guide. Organizational Research Methods. doi:10.1177/10944281261469432.

Skinner, C. J. (1989). Domain means, regression and multivariate analysis. In C. J. Skinner, D. Holt, & T. M. F. Smith (Eds.), Analysis of complex surveys (pp. 59–87). Wiley.

Asparouhov, T. (2005). Sampling weights in latent variable modeling. Structural Equation Modeling, 12, 411–434. doi:10.1207/s15328007sem1203_4.

Fraley, C., & Raftery, A. E. (2007). Bayesian regularization for normal mixture estimation and model-based clustering. Journal of Classification, 24, 155–181. doi:10.1007/s00357-007-0004-5.

See also

multilca() for a model in which every indicator is categorical.

Examples

# Course sessions nested in students: engagement profiles of sessions, and
# classes of students that differ in how often they are engaged.
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
fit <- multilpa(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 4,
                seed = 42)
summary(fit)
